**A Thousand Words, Spent Freely**

The first thing that comes is the strangeness of the invitation itself. A thousand words, no subject, no constraint except the count. It's like being handed a small plot of land and told: grow anything. Most of life isn't like this. Most words are spoken in service of something—an answer, an apology, a transaction, a request to pass the salt. To be given words with no assignment attached is to be reminded that language can be a place you wander rather than a road you take to get somewhere.

So let me wander.

I keep thinking about windowsills. Specifically, the things people put on them: a jade plant in a chipped mug, a smooth stone carried home from a beach whose name has been forgotten, a candle burned down to a stub but never thrown away. Windowsills are where we put objects that have no function except to be looked at occasionally, half-noticed, while we're doing something else. They are little museums of the unimportant. And yet if you asked someone to throw away the stone, they'd hesitate. The hesitation is the interesting part. It means the stone is doing work after all—holding a day in place, anchoring a memory that would otherwise drift off. We surround ourselves with small mnemonic ballast and call it clutter.

This is, I think, what attention does generally. It turns ordinary things into keepsakes. The beach had ten thousand stones; the one on the windowsill is special only because someone bent down. Bending down is the whole secret. Almost nothing is interesting from a standing position, at walking speed, on the way to somewhere else. But crouch next to anything—a patch of moss, a stranger's sentence, your own irritation—and it opens up like a hinged box. The moss becomes a forest. The sentence becomes a biography. The irritation becomes a map of what you actually care about, which is rarely what you thought.

Here is something else that comes to me: the way time behaves differently depending on what you fill it with. An hour of waiting is enormous, gray, geological. An hour of conversation with someone you love is a coin that slips through a hole in your pocket. We say time flies or drags as if time were the variable, but time is the only constant in the equation. We're the variable. The hour is always sixty minutes of the universe doing exactly what it does; what changes is how porous we are to it. Boredom is a kind of waterproofing. Joy is absorbency.

And memory makes it stranger still, because memory reverses the exchange rate. The boring years compress to a sentence—"I worked there for a while"—and the vivid afternoon expands to fill whole rooms of the mind. So if you want a long life, in the only sense that matters retrospectively, the strategy is clear: collect vivid afternoons. Do the thing that will be a story. The days that are all alike merge into one day; the day that is unlike any other gets to keep its name.

I think about how much of human wisdom is just this point, restated. *Be here now. Stop and smell the roses. Carpe diem.* The advice survives every century because every century ignores it, and every century ignores it because attention is expensive and the world keeps presenting cheaper options. It is easier to skim than to read, easier to scroll than to sit, easier to have opinions than experiences. None of this is a moral failing exactly. It's gravity. The remarkable thing is not that people get distracted but that anyone, ever, manages to be fully somewhere—and that when they do, they almost always describe it afterward as the point of everything.

Let me spend some of my remaining words on a small scene, because abstractions need furniture.

A man is teaching his daughter to skip stones. The lake is flat and pewter-colored, early evening. She is maybe seven, and her throws are catastrophes—stones that plunge straight down with an embarrassed *ploonk*. He shows her the grip, the sidearm, the wrist. He says, "You're throwing it *at* the water. You have to throw it *along* the water." She doesn't understand, and then, on the fourteenth try, she does—not in her head but in her arm. The stone touches down, lifts, touches again. Three skips. She screams as if she's won something, and she has. The man will forget most of that year. He will not forget the three skips. Neither will she, although in her memory the lake will be bigger, the light more golden, and her father younger than he probably was. Memory is not a recording. It is a painting, and the painter loves you.

What strikes me about that scene—why it surfaced, maybe—is that nothing in it is useful. The skill of skipping stones has no application. The lake doesn't care. And yet it's exactly the kind of moment that, multiplied, constitutes a life worth having had. We are strange creatures: we organize our days around the useful and our memories around the useless. Perhaps that's the correction the heart applies to the calendar. The calendar says the meeting mattered. The heart keeps the lake.

I have a few words left, so I'll end where I started: with the gift of an unassigned space. You gave me a thousand words and no instructions, and what came was windowsills, the elasticity of hours, a girl and a stone. I notice that everything that arrived, arrived small. Maybe that's the lesson freedom teaches when it's given in limited quantity: with infinite room you might attempt cathedrals, but with a thousand words you reach for what fits in a hand. A stone. A stub of candle. Three skips across pewter water.

If you have a windowsill, look at it today. Everything on it is a day you bent down for. That's not clutter. That's the proof you were here.
